extracted.intended_audience: students and problem-solvers studying combinatorics/invariance/coloring proofs (math-olympiad / advanced high-school and undergraduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and standards for proving impossibility or reachability in discrete combinatorial problems using invariants, parity/coloring, weight assignments, pigeonhole, and related counting/structural arguments. The page is a textbook chapter giving many exemplar methods and short worked solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference W − B invariant (color-sum difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of T does not change the difference W − B (sum of numbers on white squares minus sum on black squares).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a two-color (chessboard) coloring and show that a move preserves the difference between totals on the two colors; compare initial and target values to show impossibility (illustrated in the text for Fig. 1.7 and Fig. 1.8 where differences 5 and −1 cannot be connected).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of ±1 labels as invariant
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace each + by +1 and each − by −1, and form the product P of all the numbers. Obviously, P is an invariant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labeling with multiplicative ±1 and tracking the product shows parity-like multiplicative invariants; use to rule out target configurations when product changes would be required (Problem 49).

rubrics_metrics.name: Associative/commutative operation invariance (order independence)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a binary operation ◦ on symbols is commutative and associative (with table e◦e=e, e◦a=a, a◦a=b, etc.), the product of all letters is independent of the order they are multiplied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model transformations as combining elements under an associative, commutative operation; then the global combination (product) is invariant under order of operations (Problem 50).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariant modulo k (heads mod 3 or remainders mod 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of heads is invariant mod 3 (or transformations leave remainder on division by 3 invariant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track counts modulo a small integer to show impossibility: if initial count ≡ r (mod k) and target count ≡ s (mod k) with r≠s, goal unattainable (Problems 51 and 55).

rubrics_metrics.name: Position-sum double-counting / divisibility condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Label positions pk (position of first integer k). By counting position numbers twice one obtains sum relations leading to P = n(3n+1)/4, which must be integer, giving n ≡ 0,1 (mod 4) as a necessary condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use double-counting of positions and divisibility constraints to derive necessary congruence conditions for arrangements (Problem 52).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomial discriminant as invariant
rubrics_metrics.description: The discriminant D = b^2 − 4ac (equivalently a^2(x1 − x2)^2) is invariant under the given transformations; different discriminants (9 and 5) imply goals cannot be reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When transformations preserve root differences or change coefficients in a controlled way, compute discriminant to decide reachability (Problem 53).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadratic-form invariant involving auxiliary quantity (gain g)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define I = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 − 2g where g is current gain; show a move leaves I unchanged. Another invariant I = ab + bc + ca + g also works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce an auxiliary variable (gain or similar) and craft a quadratic or symmetric polynomial in the variables plus the auxiliary so that moves cancel out, yielding an invariant to constrain possible outcomes (Problem 54).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight-assignment invariant (geometric weights)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign weight 2^{−m−n} to a chip on square (m,n). Cutting a triangle corresponds to replacing a chip at (m,n) by chips at (m+1,n) and (m,n+1); total weight is invariant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign exponentially decaying weights to elements placed on a lattice so that legal moves preserve total weight; compare initial and hypothetical final weights to show impossibility (Problem 56).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariant for recurrence sequences (product or ratio invariants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare xn+1/xn and yn+1/yn to find an invariant such as x_n^2 y_n = a^2 b; show monotone bounds and common limits to deduce conclusions about limits and invariant values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For iterative sequences, look for multiplicative or rational combinations that remain constant across steps; use monotonicity to find limits and deduce numeric constraints (Problem 57).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted index sum modulo k invariant for words
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign I(W) = a1 + 2a2 + 3a3 + ··· + n an to a word W; deletion or insertion of any word XXX produces Z with I(W) ≡ I(Z) (mod 3). Since I(01) ≡ 2 and I(10) ≡ 1, goal cannot be attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use weighted position sums (modulo small k) to track how block insertions/deletions affect a global invariant, ruling out target strings (Problem 58).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum-difference invariant for partitioned vertices
rubrics_metrics.description: Select four vertices with no edges between them; let X be sum on these and Y sum on remaining vertices. A step does not change I = X − Y (initially ±1), so certain targets cannot be attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partition vertices into two complementary sets and show moves preserve difference of sums to forbid reaching certain configurations (Problem 59).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariant involving reciprocals of sequences (linear combination invariant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider sequences s_n = 1/x_n and t_n = 1/y_n. An invariant is s_{n+1} + 2 t_{n+1} = s_n + 2 t_n = 1/a + 2/b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes linear combinations of reciprocals (or other transforms) are constant; identify and use them to tie together initial parameters and all subsequent states (Problem 60).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-color chessboard parity coloring for domino-style tilings
rubrics_metrics.description: Each domino covers one black and one white square. Removing two opposite corners (same color) leaves unequal numbers of black/white squares, making a perfect domino cover impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Color the board in two colors and use the invariant that each domino covers one of each color; compare counts to show impossibility (mutilated chessboard example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tile-specific color-pattern counting (tetromino / polyomino)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how many squares of each color a given tile occupies (e.g., T-tetromino covers 3 of one color and 1 of the other). Use parity and count of tiles to get contradictions (Problems 2–5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Color the board appropriately (often chessboard or multi-color) so that each tile type has a fixed color-multiset; global color counts then impose constraints on how many tiles of each type can be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagonal/mod-k coloring for polyomino tiling arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Color the board diagonally in k colors (0,1,...,k−1) so that certain tiles always cover each color in a fixed multiset (e.g., straight tetromino covers one of each color in mod-4 coloring).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use k-color diagonal or modular colorings to show that a required uniform distribution of colors is impossible given board counts (Problems 5, 10, 26).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate-sum mod k coloring for higher-dimensional packings
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign color i to cell (x,y,z) if x+y+z ≡ i (mod 4). A 1×1×4 brick always occupies one cell of each color, so required equal counts per color constrain packability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use coordinate-sum modular coloring to force each placement to occupy all residue classes and compare global counts to show packing impossibility (Problem 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisibility necessary condition for 1×n tilings (n | a or n | b)
rubrics_metrics.description: An a×b rectangle can be covered by 1×n rectangles iff n divides a or n divides b. Coloring and residual-count arguments give the necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partition by colors or residues along one axis, count coverage by horizontal/vertical tiles, deduce divisibility constraints from remainders (Problem 8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternating-column/row coloring for minimum-empty-square problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Color columns alternately black and white; moving diagonally changes color, so count of color-changes gives lower bounds on free squares (Problem 12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate colorings are useful to bound how many squares must become empty or occupied after simultaneous moves that change colors predictably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole / box principle with row/column colorings to force monochromatic rectangles
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider lattice points with 1 ≤ x ≤ n+1, 1 ≤ y ≤ n^{n+1}+1; by pigeonhole at least two rows have same coloring and produce a monochromatic rectangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use combinatorial counting of row colorings (or more general color patterns) to guarantee repeated patterns and extract monochromatic substructures (Problem 13).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric color-forcing via constructed configurations
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct geometric figures (pyramids, prisms, circles of points at fixed distances) to force the existence of same-colored unit-distance configurations (Problems 14, 17, 18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geometric constructions and symmetry/rotation to propagate colors and find required same-color distances or derive contradictions when assumed impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lattice parity coloring for reflection-invariance
rubrics_metrics.description: Color lattice points black/white so that reflections preserve color (e.g., points with odd coordinates black). By reflections you always stay on lattices of same color, so opposite vertex cannot be reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When allowed operations are reflections (or other parity-preserving transforms), color by coordinate parity to identify invariant classes (Problem 23).

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangulation + 3-coloring for art-gallery watchman bound
rubrics_metrics.description: Triangulate a simple n-gon and properly 3-color the triangulation vertices; choose the color that occurs least. Watchmen at those vertices (≤ n/3) surveil all walls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triangulate and use graph coloring to produce small dominating/cover sets; this yields the classic n/3 guard bound (Problem 25).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fault-line counting argument for domino tilings
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential fault-lines (lines that cut the rectangle without cutting dominoes) must be broken by tiles; if a fault-line is broken by a single tile, complementary regions become untileable. Counting gives contradictions (Problem 28).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how tiles intersect potential separating lines; show each such line must be broken multiple times and derive area contradictions to rule out tilings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign-product parity argument for ±1 matrices
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ai be product of row i, bj product of column j. Show sum a1+b1+...+a25+b25 = 0 leads to parity contradiction because numbers of negative row/column products have opposite parity, making the total product signs incompatible (Problem 29).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute row/column sign-products and compare parities to obtain contradictions when global product constraints are imposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Block (submatrix) coloring arguments for locating single tiles
rubrics_metrics.description: Color with 3 colors 0,1,2 so that each 3×1 tile covers a fixed color-pattern; show that if all 0-squares were covered by 1×3 tiles counts of other colors contradict, forcing the monomino to occupy a 0-square (Problem 26).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design a coloring so that the target single tile must occupy a special color-class to balance global color counts; use counting to narrow allowable positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3D subcube parity coloring for packing contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition a 6×6×6 cube into 2×2×2 subcubes colored in checkerboard fashion: counts of black and white unit cubes differ so that 1×1×4 bricks (using 2 black, 2 white) cannot fill the box with given number of bricks (Problem 30).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group unit cubes into larger parity-colored blocks to create imbalance contradictions when bricks use fixed color-multisets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Row/column alternating coloring for divisibility by k arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Color rows alternately black/white so that certain tiles (2×2, 3×3, etc.) cover predictable black/white differences; use divisibility/mod arguments (e.g., difference divisible by 3) to obtain contradictions (Problem 32).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose alternation period equal to tile dimension or modulus k to expose invariant congruence properties of the tiling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternating-vertex traversal parity obstruction
rubrics_metrics.description: On certain walks or tours (e.g., visiting vertices and centers alternately), parity or alternation counts (8 vertices vs 6 faces) make the required alternating sequence impossible (Problem 33).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When moves must alternate between two types of positions, compare the counts of each type to see if a closed tour is feasible.
